title: LCA of Flexible Plastic Food Packaging: Multilayer, Mono-material and Paper-based Pouches
sub: A cradle-to-grave assessment of a coffee pouch, showing how barrier performance, food waste and design-for-recycling interact.
pdf: Case 06 — LCA of Flexible Food Packaging: Executive Summary
fu: Packaging to protect and deliver 250 g of ground coffee to a household in Germany, with a 12-month shelf life
ref: Baseline: one 11 g multilayer PET/aluminium/PE pouch with degassing valve. Alternatives: 10 g mono-material PE pouch with EVOH barrier; 14 g paper-based pouch with barrier coating; mono-PE with 30% recycled content
boundary: Cradle-to-grave including food waste attributable to packaging performance: polymer and foil production, film extrusion, printing, lamination, filling, distribution, use (coffee lost due to barrier failure), collection, recycling, energy recovery and disposal
geo: Packaging produced and filled in Germany; use and end-of-life in Germany
method: EF 3.1 characterisation; IPCC AR6 GWP100; AWARE for water scarcity
alloc: Coffee production burdens (≈6 kg CO2e/kg) included only for the share of coffee wasted because of packaging performance; recycling via cut-off with incineration of non-recycled fractions
cutoff: Flows <1% of mass and energy excluded (adhesive residues, valve components below 0.2 g) with cumulative exclusions <5%
dq: PlasticsEurope eco-profiles, ecoinvent, CEFLEX guidance, published food-waste-packaging studies; food-waste rates are assumptions. Overall data quality Medium; Low for food-waste rates
srcShort: Illustrative model; parameters within ranges from PlasticsEurope, ecoinvent, CEFLEX D4ACE guidelines and published packaging–food waste LCA studies.
loop: Circular loop: mono-material PE pouches recycled into film or non-food applications
exec:
This case study assesses a pouch for 250 g of ground coffee and compares a conventional multilayer PET/aluminium/PE laminate with a mono-material PE pouch, a paper-based pouch and a mono-PE pouch with recycled content. Flexible packaging is light and protective but hard to recycle; the EU Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation requires all packaging to be recyclable by 2030.
The illustrative baseline result is 0.091 kg CO2e per pack, including coffee lost through barrier failure. Material production (especially aluminium foil) contributes 38%, and incineration at end-of-life 22%, because the multilayer pouch cannot be recycled. Coffee wasted through packaging failure adds 16%.
The mono-material PE pouch reduces the result by 25% to 0.068 kg CO2e, and to 0.061 kg with 30% recycled content. The paper-based pouch has a lower material footprint but, with a weaker barrier assumed to raise coffee waste to 3%, its total (0.090 kg) is almost the same as the baseline.
The central finding is that packaging must be assessed together with the product it protects. Recommendations favour mono-material designs with proven barrier performance. For CSRD, results support ESRS E5 (recyclability and recycled content), E1 (Scope 3) and E2 (plastic pollution).
overview:
Ground coffee needs a high oxygen and moisture barrier to keep its aroma. Traditionally this has been achieved with laminates combining PET, aluminium foil and PE, which perform well but cannot be separated for recycling.
The purpose of this LCA is to compare redesign options and to make visible the trade-off between packaging impacts and food waste, which is often ignored when packaging is switched to materials perceived as greener.
goal: The goal is to support a coffee brand's packaging redesign under the PPWR recyclability requirements. The audience is packaging development, sustainability and procurement teams. Results are for internal decisions; any public comparison would require critical review.

stages.what: Production of PET, LDPE, aluminium foil (or EVOH, paper and coatings in alternatives).
stages.em: CO2 from energy and feedstock; aluminium smelting emissions
stages.as: 2 g aluminium foil at global-average intensity

stages.what: Films are extruded and reverse-printed with solvent-based inks.
Layers are laminated with adhesives and converted into stand-up pouches with valves.
Coffee is filled under nitrogen flushing and heat-sealed.
stages.as: Coffee production outside the boundary except for wasted coffee

stages.what: Transport to retail distribution centres and stores.
Coffee that goes stale or is spoiled because of barrier or seal failure is discarded.
stages.in: Coffee production burden for wasted share
stages.wa: Coffee waste to biowaste or residual
stages.as: 1% loss for high barrier; 3% for paper-based barrier (illustrative)

stages.what: Pouches go to yellow-bin collection; multilayers are sorted out and incinerated, mono-PE can be recycled.
stages.as: Multilayer 0% recycled; mono-PE 50% recycled; paper-based 70% recycled

lci: Coffee lost due to packaging performance

hot.why: Aluminium is about a fifth of the pouch mass but around half its material footprint, and it blocks recycling of the laminate.
Burning fossil-based plastic releases CO2; the multilayer pouch has no realistic recycling route.
Each 1% of coffee lost adds about 0.015 kg CO2e, which is comparable to the entire production of the pouch film layers.
Adhesives and solvents add energy use and VOC emissions; solvent-free lamination is available.

desc: 11 g laminate with aluminium foil; 1% coffee loss; incinerated
10 g recyclable PE pouch with EVOH barrier; 1.2% coffee loss; 50% recycled
14 g paper with barrier coating; 3% coffee loss due to weaker barrier; 70% recycled
As mono-PE with 30% post-consumer recycled PE in non-food-contact layers

sens.t: Sensitivity: coffee lost because of packaging performance
sens.xl: Share of coffee wasted due to packaging (%)
sens.note: Food waste rate is the most uncertain parameter and can reverse rankings. Lines show each design across the full range of loss rates.
sens.interp: The paper-based pouch is lower only if its food-loss rate stays within about 2 percentage points of the multilayer pouch. Barrier testing should precede any switch.

ci.stage: Material production and incineration together account for 60% of the baseline; coffee lost in use adds 16%.
ci.stage_e: Fossil feedstock in polymers and aluminium dominates energy demand.
ci.stage_w: Water is embodied mainly in wasted coffee and in material production.
ci.donut: Design decisions (materials, recyclability) influence about three quarters of the result; food protection influences the rest.
ci.sankey: All 11 g of the multilayer pouch leave the system as residual waste; none returns as material.
ci.heat: Material production is the hotspot for climate, energy and resources; wasted coffee is a hotspot for water, land and eutrophication.
ci.scen: Mono-material PE reduces the result by a quarter; the paper-based pouch loses its advantage through higher coffee loss.
ci.radar: The paper-based pouch scores worst on water, land and eutrophication because of wasted coffee, despite lower fossil material use.
ci.wf: Removing the aluminium layer and enabling recycling deliver most of the reduction; a small increase in food loss partly offsets gains.

interp.m: Packaging that protects food well can have a lower total footprint than a lighter or more recyclable option that leads to more waste. Mono-material designs with proven barriers offer the best balance here.
interp.a: Food-loss rates by design; coffee footprint per kg; recycling yields for mono-PE; aluminium foil intensity.
interp.u: Food-loss rates are rarely measured and are the dominant uncertainty; actual recycling of flexible films in practice is still developing.
interp.can: Removing aluminium and designing for recycling lowers impact if barrier performance is maintained; food protection must be part of any packaging comparison.
interp.cannot: The study cannot say that paper-based packaging is worse in general; a paper pouch with equal barrier performance would perform well.
interp.d: Selection of redesign options for PPWR recyclability, barrier testing requirements, recycled-content targets.

recs: Follow design-for-recycling guidelines (e.g., CEFLEX D4ACE): mono-PE or mono-PP with thin barrier layers; test shelf life before switching.
Request recyclability certification and shelf-life test data from converters; specify post-consumer recycled content where food-safety rules allow.
Adopt solvent-free lamination and renewable energy; reduce converting waste.
Avoid de-listing protective packaging for appearance reasons; communicate correct disposal.
Invest in flexible-film sorting and recycling; develop quality standards for film recyclate.
Report recyclability (PPWR grade) and recycled content in E5; include food-waste effects in packaging decisions.
Align recyclability criteria with food-protection needs; support film recycling infrastructure.

take: Packaging protects products: a recyclable mono-material pouch cuts the coffee pack's footprint by a quarter, while a paper-based pouch with a weaker barrier can erase its own savings through extra coffee waste.
biz: Move to mono-material pouches with tested barrier performance, set recycled-content targets where food-safety rules allow, and require shelf-life evidence before adopting any alternative material.
assume: Coffee footprint 6 kg CO2e/kg; 1% coffee loss for high-barrier designs and 3% for paper-based (illustrative); mono-PE 50% recycled; multilayer 0%; cut-off allocation.
